title: Bitwise Operations
summary: Work with binary directly: AND, OR, XOR, AND NOT, shifts, single-bit tricks, and flags built with iota.
intro: Every integer is a row of bits, and Go lets you work on them directly. Bit operations pack many yes or no values into one number, power flags and permissions, and solve some classic puzzles in a single pass. Go spells two of them its own way: `^x` is NOT and `&^` is AND NOT.

steps.title: AND, OR, XOR, AND NOT
steps.body:
Bitwise operators work on the single bits of an integer. Use `uint8` (the same type as `byte`) when you want exactly 8 bits, and print it with `%08b`: binary, padded with zeros to 8 digits, so every bit shows.

```go
var a, b uint8 = 12, 10   // 00001100 and 00001010
fmt.Printf("%08b\n", a&b) // 00001000
```

Each operator compares the two values bit by bit:

- `a & b` (AND) keeps the bits set in both.
- `a | b` (OR) keeps the bits set in either.
- `a ^ b` (XOR) keeps the bits set in exactly one.
- `a &^ b` (AND NOT) keeps the bits of `a` that are not set in `b`. It clears the bits of `b` out of `a`.

`&^` is one operator, special to Go. Write binary literals with `0b`, so `0b1010` is 10. Use unsigned types for bit masks: a negative `int` prints with `%b` as a minus sign followed by the bits of its absolute value (`-101` for -5), not as the raw bits in memory.

example.title: Comparing 12 and 10
example.prompt: Read two bytes and print each bitwise combination in binary and decimal.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var a, b uint8
	fmt.Scan(&a, &b)
	fmt.Printf("and: %08b %d\n", a&b, a&b)
	fmt.Printf("or: %08b %d\n", a|b, a|b)
	fmt.Printf("xor: %08b %d\n", a^b, a^b)
	fmt.Printf("and not: %08b %d\n", a&^b, a&^b)
	fmt.Println(0b1010)
}
example.explanation: `fmt.Scan` reads 12 and 10 straight into the `uint8` variables. Lined up, 12 is `00001100` and 10 is `00001010`. Only bit 3 is on in both, so AND gives 8. OR collects bits 1, 2, and 3 for 14. XOR drops bit 3, which both share, and keeps 6. AND NOT starts from `a` and removes every bit that `b` has, leaving bit 2, which is 4. The last line shows that the literal `0b1010` is just the number 10.

practice.title: Permission masks
practice.prompt:
Compare two permission masks bit by bit.

1. Read two numbers into `uint8` variables `a` and `b` with `fmt.Scan`.
2. Print `both:`, then `a & b` with `%08b`, then its decimal value.
3. Print `either:` the same way for `a | b`.
4. Print `first only:` for `a &^ b`.
5. Print `second only:` for `b &^ a`.

Input:

```text
240 170
```

Expected output:

```text
both: 10100000 160
either: 11111010 250
first only: 01010000 80
second only: 00001010 10
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var a, b uint8
	fmt.Scan(&a, &b)
	fmt.Printf("both: %08b %d\n", a&b, a&b)
	fmt.Printf("either: %08b %d\n", a|b, a|b)
	fmt.Printf("first only: %08b %d\n", a&^b, a&^b)
	fmt.Printf("second only: %08b %d\n", b&^a, b&^a)
}

tests.output:
both: 00000001 1
either: 00000111 7
first only: 00000100 4
second only: 00000010 2

hints: Pass the same expression twice: `fmt.Printf("both: %08b %d\n", a&b, a&b)`.
`a &^ b` and `b &^ a` are different: each keeps the bits of its left side that the right side lacks.

steps.title: Shifts and single bits
steps.body:
Shifts slide every bit left or right. `x << n` multiplies by 2 to the n, and `x >> n` divides by 2 to the n, rounding down, for non-negative `x`. Bits pushed past either end are lost, so in a `uint8`, `200 << 1` is 144, not 400. Gotcha: shifting a negative `int` right keeps the sign, so `-7 >> 1` is -4, not -3.

`1 << i` is a mask with only bit i on (bits count from 0 at the right). Combine it with `&`, `|`, `^`, and `&^` (AND, OR, XOR, and AND NOT) to work on one bit:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var x, i uint8 = 5, 1
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println("bit was on:", on)
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", x)
}
```

```go
on := x>>i&1 == 1 // check bit i
x |= 1 << i       // set bit i
x &^= 1 << i      // clear bit i
x ^= 1 << i       // toggle bit i
```

In Go, `<<`, `>>`, and `&` bind tighter than `==`, so `x>>i&1 == 1` needs no parentheses. Unary `^x` flips every bit (NOT). Go has no `~` operator. If `x` is a `uint8` holding 5, `^x` is 250. If `x` is an `int` holding 5, `^x` is -6, because the flipped top bit is the sign bit.

example.title: Flipping single bits
example.prompt: Shift a byte, then set, check, toggle, clear, and flip its bits.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var x, i uint8
	fmt.Scan(&x, &i)
	fmt.Println(x<<2, x>>1)
	x |= 1 << i
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", x)
	fmt.Println(x>>0&1 == 1)
	x ^= 1 << 1
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", x)
	x &^= 1 << i
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", x)
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", ^x)
}
example.explanation: With x = 5 (`00000101`), `x<<2` is 5 times 4 and `x>>1` is 5 divided by 2, truncated. Setting bit 3 ORs in `00001000`. Bit 0 is on, so the check prints `true`. Toggling bit 1 turns it on because it was off. Clearing bit 3 with `&^=` removes it again. `^x` returns a new value with all 8 bits flipped and leaves `x` itself unchanged. The untyped constant `1` in `1 << i` takes the type of `x`, so every mask here is a `uint8` too.

practice.title: Light switches
practice.prompt:
Control a row of 8 lights stored in one byte.

1. Read the light pattern and a light number into `uint8` variables with `fmt.Scan`.
2. Print the pattern shifted left by 1 and shifted right by 2, as decimals on one line separated by a space.
3. Turn the chosen light on and print the pattern with `%08b`.
4. Print whether light 7 is on (`true` or `false`).
5. Toggle light 0 and print the pattern.
6. Turn the chosen light off and print the pattern.
7. Print every light flipped with `^`, as `%08b`.

Input:

```text
6 4
```

Expected output:

```text
12 1
00010110
false
00010111
00000111
11111000
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var lights, n uint8
	fmt.Scan(&lights, &n)
	fmt.Println(lights<<1, lights>>2)
	lights |= 1 << n
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", lights)
	fmt.Println(lights>>7&1 == 1)
	lights ^= 1 << 0
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", lights)
	lights &^= 1 << n
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", lights)
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", ^lights)
}
hints: The shifts work like in the example. In a `uint8`, bits pushed past the left end are lost.
Build a mask with only light n on as `1 << n`, then combine it with `|=`, `^=`, or `&^=`.
To check light 7, shift it down to bit 0 and keep only that bit with `& 1`, then compare with 1.

steps.title: Flags with iota
steps.body:
A set of yes or no options fits in one number: give each option its own bit. `1 << iota` in a `const` block makes the powers of two for you, because each line repeats the expression with the next `iota`.

```go
const (
	Read  = 1 << iota // 1 (001)
	Write             // 2 (010)
	Exec              // 4 (100)
)
```

Then the bit operators become flag operations:

- `perm := Read | Write` combines flags.
- `perm&Write != 0` tests a flag.
- `perm |= Exec` adds a flag.
- `perm &^= Write` removes a flag.

Unlike C, Go gives `&` higher precedence than `!=`, so `perm&Write != 0` needs no parentheses. Removing with `&^=` is safe even when the flag is already off, while subtracting would break the mask. In memory, a `uint8` mask holds 8 flags in one byte, where 8 `bool` variables take 8 bytes. That is why file modes and option sets are passed around as masks.

example.title: File permissions
example.prompt: Read a permission mask, report each flag, then add Write and remove Exec.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

const (
	Read = 1 << iota
	Write
	Exec
)

func main() {
	var perm uint8
	fmt.Scan(&perm)
	fmt.Println("Read:", perm&Read != 0)
	fmt.Println("Write:", perm&Write != 0)
	fmt.Println("Exec:", perm&Exec != 0)
	perm |= Write
	perm &^= Exec
	fmt.Printf("%03b\n", perm)
}
example.output:
Read: true
Write: false
Exec: true
011
example.explanation: The constants are 1, 2, and 4, one bit each. The mask 5 is `101`, so Read and Exec are on and Write is off. `perm |= Write` adds bit 1 to make `111`, and `perm &^= Exec` clears bit 2, leaving `011`. `%03b` pads the binary to 3 digits, one per flag. The constants are untyped, so they work with the `uint8` mask without any conversion.

practice.title: Pizza toppings
practice.prompt:
Edit a pizza order stored as a topping mask.

1. Declare `Cheese`, `Ham`, `Olives`, and `Peppers`, in that order, with `1 << iota`.
2. Read the mask into a `uint8` variable with `fmt.Scan`.
3. Print the name of each topping that is on, one per line, in declaration order.
4. Add Olives with `|=` and remove Ham with `&^=`.
5. Print the final mask with `%04b`.

Input:

```text
3
```

Expected output:

```text
Cheese
Ham
0101
```
hints: Only the first constant needs `= 1 << iota`. The lines after it repeat the expression.
Use one `if mask&Flag != 0` per topping, in order.
With mask 0 no topping prints, and only the final mask line appears.

steps.title: Bit tricks and math/bits
steps.body:
XOR has a handy property: `x ^ x` is 0 and `x ^ 0` is `x`. XOR every value of a list together, and any value that appears twice cancels itself out, in any order. What is left is the value without a pair.

Two more classic tricks use `n - 1`, which flips the lowest set bit and every zero below it:

- `n & (n-1)` clears the lowest set bit (12 `1100` becomes 8 `1000`).
- `n > 0 && n&(n-1) == 0` tests for a power of two, since those have exactly one bit set. The `n > 0` part rules out 0.

The `math/bits` package counts bits for you. Its functions take a `uint`, so convert first:

```go
import "math/bits"

bits.OnesCount(uint(12)) // 2 set bits
bits.Len(uint(12))       // 4 bits needed to write 1100
```

`bits.Len(0)` is 0. Convert only non-negative values: `uint(-1)` wraps to the largest `uint`, with all 64 bits set. The compiler turns both functions into one or two CPU instructions on most machines, so they beat a loop over the bits.

example.title: The lonely number
example.prompt: Find the one value without a pair, then report its bit count, bit length, and whether it is a power of two.
example.explanation: The loop XORs each number into `single` until `fmt.Scan` returns an error at the end of input. The two 7s and the two 3s cancel, so 5 is left. 5 is `101`: two set bits, and 3 bits long. `5 & 4` is 4, not 0, so 5 is not a power of two. `uint(single)` converts the `int` because the `bits` functions take a `uint`.

practice.title: Unpaired sock
practice.prompt:
Find the unpaired number and describe its bits.

1. Read numbers until the input ends, where every value appears twice except one.
2. XOR them all together to find the unpaired value.
3. Add `"math/bits"` to the imports.
4. Print, on one line separated by spaces: the value, its set-bit count, its bit length, the value with its lowest set bit cleared (`n & (n-1)`), and whether it is a power of two (`true` or `false`).

Input:

```text
4 1 2 1 2
```

Expected output:

```text
4 1 3 0 true
```
hints: Inside the loop, XOR each number into `single` with `^=`.
Test for a power of two like the example does. Without the `single > 0` check, 0 would wrongly count as a power of two.

recap:
- Use `uint8` for 8-bit values and print them with `%08b` to see every bit.
- `&` keeps bits set in both, `|` in either, `^` in exactly one, and `&^` keeps the left bits the right lacks.
- `x << n` multiplies by 2 to the n and `x >> n` divides by it for non-negative `x`. Bits shifted off the end are lost.
- Check bit i with `x>>i&1 == 1`, set it with `x |= 1 << i`, clear it with `x &^= 1 << i`, and toggle it with `x ^= 1 << i`.
- Unary `^x` flips every bit. Go has no `~`.
- `1 << iota` makes flag constants. Combine with `|`, test with `perm&Flag != 0`, remove with `&^=`.
- `bits.OnesCount(uint(n))` counts set bits and `bits.Len(uint(n))` gives the bits needed.
- `x ^ x` is 0, `n & (n-1)` clears the lowest set bit, and `n > 0 && n&(n-1) == 0` tests for a power of two.
